5-6: Two clubs with some pupils in both: how many are in neither.
Everyone in one of two groups or in both: how many are in both, or in exactly one.
The fewest or the most that can be in both of two groups within a fixed total.
The largest number who could belong to neither group.
Three groups with given overlaps: how many belong to all three.
Answers to two yes-or-no questions counted in a table: the missing count.
Twice as many in both groups as in neither, or another tie between the parts: each part from it.
A small team in which most can do each of three things: the fewest who must do all three.
Counts of those who did not do something: how many did both things.
Whole numbers up to some number that divide by 2 or by 3: counted without counting any twice.
All but so many are cats and all but as many are owls, the rest of a third kind, each kind there at least once: cats and owls come out equal, and only all but two fixes the count, at one of each.
Each child holds three cards of two kinds and is counted for every word it can spell: the overlaps between the counts tell how many hold cards all of one kind.
Lists of those who solved the first problem, exactly one, at least one and both: which list is the longest, and when two lists can be the same.
Couples where a share of the men and a share of the women are married: as many married men as married women give the share of all who are married.
Boxes of a few things where every two boxes share exactly one thing: what one more box must hold to keep the rule.
